messages.subject_clean: Error with node names when compiled
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dirk,

Uncompiled execution runs in R. Code-generation for compiled execution does not handle every case of R syntax.

In this case, the model methods like getLogProb, calculate, and simulate can work with either a full vector of node names or a singly-indexed node name, but not arbitrary indexing of vectors of node names.  That's because node relationships are partially evaluated during the compilation process, so some run-time flexibility is not supported.

It is really helpful if you can provide the code related to an error.  I am guessing you have a nimbleFunction with f_dependencies in it.  But in this case I can make a guess.

I think you have something like

lp <- model$getLogProb(f_dependencies[f_start_depend[1]:f_end_depend[1]])

and you will need to replace it with

lp <- 0
for(i in f_start_depend[1]:f_end_depend[1]) {
  lp <- lp + model$getLogProb(f_dependencies[i])
}

HTH
-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Often pasting node names together works, but it is easy to make mistakes when there is more than one index involved.  "x[1, 2]" will be a valid node name but "x[1,2]" will not be.  You can put your node names through model$expandNodeNames to fix issues like that.  The order of nodes matters for model$calculate and model$simulate, but it should not matter for model$getLogProb, since that only accesses cached values of log probabilities from the last call to model$calculate.  If those comments aren't relevant to your use case, I'd need to see code or examples of the node names to guess further at what the issue might be.
-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Rob,

What do you see when you build the model and try inspecting its values?

model <- nimbleModel(<your args>)

model$ch[131, 3:17]

Often initial values are an issue.  Did you set reasonable inits for mu.lp and mu.lphi?  You can look with

model$phi
model$p

BTW, there is an expit function.

It looks like you may be setting up to elaborate with time- or site-specific explanatory pieces, but if not you can vectorize:

phi[1:(n.occ-1), s] <- expit(lphi[ 1:(n.occ-1), s]))

If you're still stuck, we can look more if you are able to send a reproducible example with some data (off-list if you prefer not to post the data publicly, but maybe only a few sites of data would be sufficient?).

Best,
-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Rob et al.,

It jumps out at me that detection probability at the  n.occ-th detection survey aren't being calculated, but are needed by dCJS_vv if last[i] ever equals n.occ.  Since dCJS conditions on first capture, I think p[first[i]] is ignored, but p[last[i]] needs to be not NA. Since you're only calculating for t in 1:(n.occ - 1), and surveys during the n.occ-th period will have p = NA unless you're directly initializing p. Is that relevant?

Ben

messages.subject: Re: Multi-state open robust design
messages.body_plain:
Hi Lisa,

I don't know if anyone has that at their fingertips.  Do you have an example of BUGS/JAGS code for it?  If so it should translate to NIMBLE easily, since we use nearly the same model language.  If you are just getting started, feel free to send the code on this list and we can advise on any tweaks for NIMBLE.  Our documentation page includes a short guide on that: https://r-nimble.org/documentation-2

You might find good resources in our set of training repositories on GitHub: https://github.com/nimble-training

These include AHMnimble, all of the BUGS/JAGS examples from Kéry and Royle's Applied Hierarchical Modeling Vol. I translated to NIMBLE.

We welcome these questions on this list, but this list is for general NIMBLE software questions.  For ecological hierarchical modeling questions, you might try the hmecology list to see if anyone has BUGS/JAGS code for your model of interest.

-Perry

Perry,
 Thanks for the tips, they'll certainly be helpful for debugging!

Rob

messages.subject: Re: Inf or NaN in BYM when zero_mean = 1
messages.subject_clean: Inf or NaN in BYM when zero_mean = 1
messages.body_plain:
Hi Gary,

(Note to others reading this, this response follows some off-list discussion in which Gary shared his data with me.)

It looks like the issue is that the 50th location has 0 neighbors and also has a 0 count. This means that the inference for phi[50] is unconstrained by the CAR prior (since there are no neighbors) and unconstrained by the data (since the likelihood increases as the mean of the Poisson for the observation at the 50th location goes to zero). So either in the zero_mean=0 or zero_mean=1 case, you will see phi[50] wandering off towards minus infinity. In the zero_mean=1 case the side effect is that the other phi values need to increase to offset phi[50].

I would suggest simply taking that location out of the modeling.

-Chris

Is there a reason you can't use the mean of the phi values in place of alpha? It really should be equivalent given you have a flat prior on alpha in your attempt with zero_mean = 1.

Hi!

I am having some issue with the fitting of the Leroux CAR model, which I cannot figure out on my own. I have followed the thread(s) in this google group on the Leroux and its conditional representation, and since my understanding is that it is not feasible because of the cycle in the corresponding DAG, I went for the joint representation:

LerouxCode <- nimbleCode(

{
for (i in 1:N){
mu_ler[i] <- mu0
O[i] ~ dpois(mu[i])
log(mu[i]) <- log(E[i]) + alpha + theta[i]
SIR[i] <- exp(alpha + theta[i])
}

# random effects
PrecMat[1:N, 1:N] <- tau.theta*(rho*Q[1:N, 1:N] + (1 - rho)*diag(N))
theta[1:N] ~ dmnorm(mean = mu_ler[1:N], prec = PrecMat[1:N,1:N])

# intercept
alpha ~ dnorm(0, tau = 1)

# precision
tau.theta ~ dgamma(1, 0.01)
sigma2.theta <- 1/tau.theta

# mixing
rho ~ dunif(0,1)
mu0 ~ dnorm(0, tau = 1/(0.001*N))
}
)

I fitted the model on the Scottish lip cancer data to see if it works and I compared it with the Leroux available in the CARBayes package.

Overall the results are fairly similar; the results for the variance parameter of the field and the mixing parameter rho are comparable. The medians of the 2 fields are also almost identical. but there are a couple of differences that bug me a bit:

The variance of the intercept alpha and the variances of the random effects theta are different between my nimble model and the CARBayes', namely my variances are substantially larger.
(minor) I have used the same priors for all parameters (except for the mixing parameter rho - my understanding is that CARBayes uses a step-base approach to get it which I wasn't sure how to replicate in nimble). Nevertheless, using the code attached, I need ~100 times more sample to reach convergence in comparison with CARBayes.

Any ideas on why the variances may be higher? I am attaching the code to fit both models.

Thanks a lot,

Tullia

Hello,
The DPMM model I'm implementing I want to be able to count the number of observations in each cluster and subset for just the actively assigned clusters in order to estimate my Poisson intensity.

Essentially for:
z[1:N] ~ dCRP(alpha, size = N)

On each iteration of the MCMC I'd like to be able to get:
ni = # of observations assigned to i = 1:M
and
yi = 0/1 if cluster i = 1:M is active.

my model is very roughly
for(j 1:N)
f(tj) ~ lambda[z[j]]/Lambda[z[j]]
for(i 1:M)
ni ~ Poisson(Lambda[i]*yi)

Is this something I have to calculate within my own nimble distribution when passing z into it? Or can I do this in a simple step within the nimble code?

I've implemented my own sampler in C++ so I know everything is kosher but it would be super cool to be able to do this in standard software. Let me know if this isn't enough information to go on.
Thanks so much!
Paul

messages.body_plain:
Hi Paul,

nice that you are using the dCRP function!

To count the number of observations per cluster and to know which are the active clusters, you would have to do it as a post processing, by looking at the MCMC’s output. This information will be in the ‘z’ vector. ‘z’ contains the assignment of observations to active clusters.  Remember to add it in the ‘monitors’ argument.

Let me ask you something: do you want to do this to do inference or to sample the intensity? I think is for the later, and if so, you shouldn’t need to do any of these things. They are already done in nimble when sampling ‘z’. Let me know if this is what you want to do so I can provide more details. Also, having more details about the nimble code would be helpful.

I hope this is useful.

Best,
Claudia

Thanks for the awesomely quick response Claudia. I love the popularity that the DPMM is getting in ecology and stoked you guys have included it in the sampler. Thanks for that! I have a very specific form of what lambda_i, the observation intensity is based on latent locations x_i, lambda(x_i).

For a known cluster K, the likelihood is from a non-homogeneous Poisson process:
exp(-sum_k=1^K (int_0^T lambda_k)) * prod_1^N lambda_i(x_i) * prod_1^K f(x_k)

However I don't observe K or the latent locations that create some unknown intensity which leads me to x_i ~ G.
For K active clusters,
The likelihood under the DPMM is then exp(-sum_k=1^K (int_0^T lambda_k)) * prod_1^N int lambda_i(x_i) dG0(x_i).

So I kind of need that extra exponential term in the MCMC to make inference on the lambda and x terms.
When I define f(t_i) as lambda(x_i)/ Lambda(x_i) where Lambda(x_i) = int_0^T lambda(x_i) dt then after I've clustered I can just call that extra term as proportional to a Poisson.

I suppose a better question is how can I incorporate the active clusters directly into my likelihood so that I can estimate that additional exponential term that is outside of the direct clustering from the CRP? Maybe this can be thought of as a hierarchical problem where there are shared parameters between the CRP and the additional terms.
Thanks so much,
Paul

messages.subject: Re: Leroux model - unexpectedly high variances
messages.body_plain:
hi Tullia,

A few thoughts here:

1) The model you are giving to nimble has both mu0 and alpha, and it looks to me like they may not be fully identified by the data. In CARbayes, it looks like only one mean parameter may be present in the model.  So trading off (negative correlation) between mu0 and alpha may explain increased variance. My suggestion would be to check carefully the specification of the mean structure of the random effects and the mean structure of the linear predictor for the Poisson and make sure they are equivalent between CARbayes and the nimble model specification.

2) When I compare tau2 from CARbayes with sigma2.theta = 1/tau.theta from nimble, it looks to me that they are equivalent.

3) As far as as nimble being much slower than CARbayes - we don't provide any sparse matrix handling at the moment, so there is a lot of inefficiency in the MCMC for the model as specified in nimble. I suspect CARbayes is taking advantage of the sparsity, though I haven't looked to see what their implementation is.

4) One side note: if you have a similar number of neighbors for each region, the Leroux model is similar to the proper CAR model (see p 1223 of https://projecteuclid.org/download/pdfview_1/euclid.ba/1570068455). Personally, I've always had trouble interpreting the Leroux model - it's not clear to me what it means to add matrices on the precision scale. So you may be able to use the proper or improper CAR models in nimble and avoid Leroux, and thereby achieve better MCMC performance in nimble.

-chris

> Hello,
>
> I am having trouble with reducing autocorrelation and increasing mixing in my MCMCs for different N-mixture models. Though the input datasets are different, I suspect that some of the underlying issues may be related.
>
> One model is a multi-species (Dorazio-Royle-Yamaura) N-mixture, and the other is a single-species (Dail-Madsen) N-mixture. In addition to MCMC autocorrelation and insufficient mixing, I have also found multimodal posteriors for many of the model parameters estimated, especially those in my process- and observation-level submodels. To date, I have not yet determined whether such problems relate to poor initialization, choices of priors, and/or choices of samplers. I have made many changes to each over the past few months.
>
> Would any users/developers be willing to please look over the enclosed model, perhaps run it, and later provide feedback on any potential issues with the initialization, choices of priors, and/or choices (or uses) of samplers?
>
> To date, I have applied RW_block (and sometimes with propCov constraints) or AF_slice samplers to problematic parameters, but I must admit that I don't know how best to fine tune the samplers toward efficient processing, especially considering the input data includes counts of both rare and common species.
>

>

> Andrew
>
> ###############################################################
>

>

>

>
>   ## Priors for community parameters
>   for(k in 1:nspec){

>     alpha2[k] ~ dnorm(mu.alpha2, sd=sd.alpha2)      # quadratic julian day on detection
>
>     ## Beta parameters (abundance)

>     beta2[k] ~ dnorm(mu.beta2, sd=sd.beta2)      # percent forb cover on abundance
>     beta3[k] ~ dnorm(mu.beta3, sd=sd.beta3)      # landscape metrics on abundance
>   }
>   tau.lam <- pow(sd.lam, -2)
>   sd.lam ~ dunif(0, 2)     # site heterogeneity in abundance
>   tau.p <- pow(sd.p, -2)
>   sd.p ~ dunif(0, 2)      # site heterogeneity in detection
>
>   ## Priors for community hyperparameters
>   for(y in 1:nyear){
>     mu.beta0[y] ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
>     sd.beta0[y] ~ dunif(0, 10)
>   }

>   sd.beta1 ~ dunif(0, 10)
>   mu.beta2 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
>   sd.beta2 ~ dunif(0, 10)
>   mu.beta3 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)

>   mu.a0L <- logit(mu.a0)
>   mu.alpha1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
>   sd.alpha1 ~ dunif(0, 10)
>   mu.alpha2 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
>   sd.alpha2 ~ dunif(0, 10)
>
>   ## Ecological model for true abundance (process model)
>   for(k in 1:nspec){

>       eps.lam[i] ~ dnorm(0, tau.lam)       spatial random effects on abundance
>       a[i,k] ~ dbern(phi[k])     # adjustment for zero-inflation
>       N[i,k] ~ dpois(a[i,k] * lambda[i,k])

>       loglam.lim[i,k] <- min(250, max(-250, loglam[i,k]))     # stabilize log
>       lambda[i,k] <- exp(loglam.lim[i,k])
>

>   }
>

>         eps.p[i] ~ dnorm(0, tau.p)      # spatial random effects on detection

>     }
>   }
>
>   for(k in 1:nspec){
>     for(y in 1:nyear){
>       mlambda[k,y] <- phi[k] * exp(beta0[k,y])     # expected abundance on natural scale
>     }
>     Nocc.fs[k] <- sum(z[1:nsite,k])     # number of occupied sites
>     logit(mp[k]) <- alpha0[k]       # mean detection on natural scale
>   }
>   for (i in 1:nsite) {

>   }
> })
>
> Ycd <- win.data$Yc
>
> nyear <- length(c(2005,2006))
> nsite <- dim(Ycd)[1]
> nrep <- (Ycd)[2]
> nspec <- dim(Ycd)[3]
>
> const <- list(year=c(rep(1,14),rep(2,14)), nyear=nyear, nsite=nsite, nrep=nrep, nspec=nspec)

>   alpha1 = rnorm(dim(Ycd)[3]),     # linear julian day on detection
>   alpha2 = rnorm(dim(Ycd)[3]),       # quadratic julian day on detection
>
>   # abundance process

>                  nrow = dim(Ycd)[3], ncol = nyear),      # abundance intercepts
>   beta1 = rnorm(dim(Ycd)[3]),      # cp type (dummy coded) on abundance
>   beta2 = rnorm(dim(Ycd)[3]),       # percent forb cover on abundance
>   beta3 = rnorm(dim(Ycd)[3]),       # landscape metrics on abundance
>
>   ## starting values for community hyperparameters
>   # detection process
>   mu.alpha0 = rnorm(1, logit(runif(1,0,1)), runif(1,0,1)),
>   mu.a0 = runif(1,0,1),
>   mu.beta0 = rnorm(2),
>   sd.beta0 = runif(2,0,5),
>   sd.alpha0 = runif(1,0,1),
>   mu.alpha1 = rnorm(1),
>   sd.alpha1 = runif(1,0,5),
>   mu.alpha2 = rnorm(1),
>   sd.alpha2 = runif(1,0,5),
>
>   # abundance process
>   mu.beta1 = rnorm(1),
>   sd.beta1 = runif(1,0,5),
>   mu.beta2 = rnorm(1),
>   sd.beta2 = runif(1,0,5),
>   mu.beta3 = rnorm(1),
>   sd.beta3 = runif(1,0,5),
>
>   # spatial random effects on abundance/detection
>   sd.lam=runif(1, 0, 2), eps.lam=rnorm(nsite),

>             "alpha0", "alpha1", "alpha2",

>
> model <- nimbleModel(code = modelCode, name = "modelCode",
>                      constants = const, data = win.data,
>                      inits = initFunction())
>
> Cmodel <- compileNimble(model)
> modelConf <- configureMCMC(model)
> modelConf$setMonitors(params)
> modelConf$removeSampler(c("alpha0","alpha1","alpha2","beta0","beta1","beta2","beta3","p"))

> modelConf$addSampler(target = c("alpha1[1:35]","alpha2[1:35]"), type = "RW_block")
> modelConf$addSampler(target = c("alpha0[1:35]"), type = "RW_block")
>
> modelMCMC <- buildMCMC(modelConf)
> CmodelMCMC <- compileNimble(modelMCMC, project = model)
>
> ni <- 10000 ; nb <- 5000 ; nt <- 5 ; nc <- 3 ; set.seed <- 999
> results <- runMCMC(CmodelMCMC, niter=ni, nburnin=nb, thin=nt, nchains=nc,

>

I think that I may be on a better track now.

Best,
Andrew

Thanks for your message.

The issue turned out to be a bit tricky to find but I think easy to fix. Thanks a lot for your answer (and apologies for the very late reply!).

> 1) The model you are giving to nimble has both mu0 and alpha, and it looks to me like they may not be fully identified by the data. In CARbayes, it looks like only one mean parameter may be present in the model.  So trading off (negative correlation) between mu0 and alpha may explain increased variance. I tried fitting the model without the parameter mu0 as well (and several variations of it) but it didn't make much difference...

> 2) When I compare tau2 from CARbayes with sigma2.theta = 1/tau.theta from nimble, it looks to me that they are equivalent.

Yes they are! I was referring to the variance of the posterior distributions of the random effects (I think this was probably highlighted better in the script than in my previous email...)

I suspect CARbayes is taking advantage of the sparsity, though I haven't looked to see what their implementation is.

Personally, I've always had trouble interpreting the Leroux model - it's not clear to me what it means to add matrices on the precision scale. So you may be able to use the proper or improper CAR models in nimble and avoid Leroux, and thereby achieve better MCMC performance in nimble.

Yep I see your point, however I was trying to compare different CAR models and I wanted the Leroux as one term of comparison, so I was trying to understand if there was anything substantially wrong in my implementation.

messages.subject: Re: nimbleRcall implementation of base::eigen
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tom,

eigen() is a supported function in nimble programming, so you might be able to avoid use of nimbleRcall for this need.  Please see  Table 11.3 in the User Manual.

In general if you do need a nimbleRcall like this, there are a couple of considerations. It is common to need to write a wrapper function, i.e. a function you access via nimbleRcall that calls your actual function of interest with arguments and then return value rearranged as needed. For example, if you just need the eigenvectors, a wrapper function could pick those out and return them.  The bigger issue is the returnType declaration: nimble type declarations do not include an R list of type declarations as a nimble type.  I think you could use a nimbleList data structure for this purpose.  You would have to create a nimbleList type and then use that as the declared returnType.  But you would still need to write a wrapper, so that you could convert the list returned from base::eigen into a nimbleList object to return from your wrapper.  I hope that makes sense.

But again, here's hoping that nimble's native support for eigen gives you what you need.

-Perry

So if you want to use any of these methods as of nimble version 0.10.0, please make sure to install the nimbleSMC package. Any existing code you have that uses any SMC functionality should continue to work as is.

As development work on NIMBLE has proceeded over the years, we've added additional functionality to the core nimble package, so we've reached the stage where it makes sense to break off some of the functionality into separate packages. Our goal is to make the overall NIMBLE platform more modular and therefore easier to maintain and use.

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

We've released version 0.10.1.  Version 0.10.1 is primarily a bug fix release:

 -  In particular, it fixes a bug in retrieving parameter values from distributions that was introduced in version 0.10.0. The bug can cause incorrect behavior of conjugate MCMC samplers under certain model structures (such as particular state-space models) so we strongly encourage users to upgrade to 0.10.1.
- In addition, version 0.10.1 restricts use of WAIC to the conditional version of WAIC (conditioning on all parameters directly involved in the likelihood). Previous versions of nimble gave incorrect results when not conditioning on all parameters directly involved in the likelihood (i.e., when not monitoring all such parameters). In a future version of nimble we plan to make a number of improvements to WAIC, including allowing use of marginal versions of WAIC, where the WAIC calculation integrates over random effects.

Please see the NEWS file in the installed package for more details (https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/blob/devel/packages/nimble/inst/NEWS).

- Chris Paciorek for the NIMBLE Development Team
